transcript: I'm not seeing nearly enough people talk about Primary Trust, so it is now time for me to tell you about it, because you need to go see it before it closes on July second. Primary Trust is a brand new play written by Ebony Booth, directed by Cadet Adams, who also directed one of my favorite plays last year, English. It is currently playing at the Roundabout theater's off Broadway space, the Laura Pells Theater, until the first weekend in July. It stars William Jackson Harper, who most people know from The Good Place as Kenneth, who is this bookstore worker who follows the same routine day in and day out. And all of a sudden, something happens in his life that upends that routine, and he has to face some things that he's been burying in his life. The synopsis is very vague because I don't wanna spoil anything. This play is literally reveal after reveal. I had no idea what to expect before going in, and it just really blew me away. This play diesel lot with how we process trauma after the fact, but in a almost comedic and a heartwarming way. I just really enjoyed this play. I've been seeing a lot of about trauma that just get really dark, and this one has dark moments, but ultimately is a comedy. William Jackson Harper is absolutely fantastic. I've never seen him on stage before, but this is also not a one person show, which I Definitely thought going in there's an absolutely fantastic supporting cast, especially the character actors who play multiple characters throughout the show, and it's just so entertaining to watch. This will also please at least one of you. You know who you are. But this is a show about an explicitly black character that does not deal at all with racism. Which is fine. We love those shows. But it's kind of refreshing to have a character explore other aspects of humanity that aren't just being discriminated against for who you are. This is often a trend in theater. A person of color will deal with racism in plays. Jewish plays are often about anti Semitism or the Holocaust. Female plays often have them going through some sort of assault, so it's nice to have something about trauma that is not related to any of that. I have never seen an Ebony Booth play before, but this is definitely not going to be the last. I just love how she writes dialogue and her approach to storytelling. Like I said, this. There was just so much folded up into this play, and the way that it is revealed is just fantastic. She's wearing a couple other plays, including Paris, but this is the first of hers that I've seen, and I cannot wait to follow her more. In a perfect world, this would get a limited Broadway run, but I just don't think enough people are seeing this. So please, please, Please do not miss this production. I cannot recommend it enough. It is only playing for a couple more weeks.
